analysis.one_liner: Bans ticket-buying bots that bypass purchase limits and makes sellers enforce their own rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill with bipartisan sponsorship in September 2025 and placed it on the Senate calendar, where it awaits floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill bans using automated software ('bots') to buy event tickets by getting around a website's security controls and posted purchase limits. It also requires online ticket sellers to maintain working systems to enforce their own purchase limits, report known bot circumvention to the Federal Trade Commission within 30 days, and fix the holes that let bots through. The FTC gains explicit power to sue violators and seek civil penalties, must set up a way for fans to file complaints, and must report enforcement results to Congress. The bill strengthens the existing 2016 anti-bot law, which already outlawed ticket bots but produced limited enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary fans trying to buy tickets at face value. Bots operated by professional resellers buy up large blocks of tickets the moment they go on sale, then resell them at a markup; by outlawing circumvention of purchase limits and making sellers enforce those limits, the bill aims to keep more tickets available to regular buyers. The FTC also gains a complaint channel and new penalty authority, and state attorneys general receive information about circumvention incidents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fans buying event tickets at face value

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful to use an automated application to purchase event tickets by circumventing an access control system, security measure, or other technological control used to enforce posted ticket purchasing order rules [S3].

Online ticket sellers must establish and maintain systems to enforce their posted purchase limits, regularly update them against new threats, and take reasonable steps to fix known causes of circumvention [S3].
Sellers must report known bot circumvention incidents to the FTC within 30 days, and the FTC must share those reports and consumer complaints with state attorneys general [S3].

The FTC gains explicit authority to bring civil actions, with penalties of at least $10,000 per day of violation, at least $1,000 per violation, and an additional $10,000 per intentional violation [S3].

The FBI, the Attorney General, and state and local law enforcement must coordinate with the FTC to share information about cyberattacks on ticket sellers' controls, and the FTC must report to Congress on enforcement status and limitations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Professional ticket resellers and bot operators, who lose the ability to harvest tickets at face value for resale at a markup. Online ticket platforms bear the cost of building and maintaining the required access controls and reporting systems.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bot-using resellers and ticket platforms' compliance costs

drawbacks.text: The 2016 BOTS Act already banned ticket bots, yet enforcement has been limited; this bill adds duties and penalties but leaves enforcement dependent on FTC resources and priorities, and it requires the FTC to report back on any limitations in its own ability to pursue circumvention cases [S3].

The version reported by the committee is narrower than the bill as introduced: it deleted the introduced requirements that sellers maintain broad 'reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards' including oversight of third-party service providers, and it added a provision barring the FTC from basing enforcement actions on its own compliance guidance [S3].

A bot ban addresses the symptom of resale markups but not other drivers of high ticket prices, such as venues and promoters releasing few tickets at face value or using market-based pricing; fans may still face high prices even if bots are curbed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For fans, the benefit is real but modest: more tickets may survive to ordinary buyers, and the FTC gets a clearer legal handle and a complaint channel. The honest caveat is that the underlying bot ban already exists, so the bill's value depends on whether the added seller duties, reporting, and penalties actually produce enforcement — and the committee-amended version dropped the introduced security-safeguard mandates, leaving the main new teeth in the penalty provisions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee favorably with an amendment in September 2025 and was placed on the Senate's legislative calendar, but the full Senate has not voted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) introduced the bill on January 22, 2025, joined by Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 30, 2025, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S5].

On September 2, 2025, the committee reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute (Report No. 119-57), and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 144 — a step that means it is eligible for Senate floor action but does not guarantee a vote [S5].

The committee-reported version narrowed the introduced bill, deleting broad security-safeguard requirements and adding a provision limiting the FTC's ability to base enforcement on its own guidance [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has gained or lost decisively: bot-driven reselling still operates under only the 2016 law's limits while the bill waits for floor time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — still awaiting a Senate vote

sides.party_line_note: A Republican lead sponsor from Tennessee and the bill's sole cosponsor, a New Mexico Democrat, advanced it together through a committee run by a Republican chair; no recorded opposition appears in the action history.

industries.industry: Professional ticket resellers and bot operators
industries.note: These businesses use automated software to grab tickets at face value and resell them at a markup; the bill outlaws the circumvention technique they rely on and attaches civil penalties starting at $10,000 per day. Their gain historically comes directly out of fans' wallets.

industries.industry: Online ticket platforms (primary sellers like Ticketmaster and secondary marketplaces)
industries.note: The bill requires platforms to build and maintain working purchase-limit controls, update them, and report circumvention incidents to the FTC within 30 days — real compliance costs. But stricter enforcement can also benefit platforms by reducing bot purchases and shifting the burden of policing resale abuse, and the committee version dropped the introduced requirements for broad security safeguards and third-party oversight.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee with bipartisan sponsorship and sits on the Senate calendar under General Orders. Bills at this stage typically advance by unanimous consent or a short floor exchange when time allows; with no recorded opposition, this one has a plausible path to Senate passage, but it would still need to pass the House and be signed before becoming law, and there is no House action in the record.
